Joy of the strong four-armed.

Women dance without skirts,  
Girls run without belts,  
Boys with half boots.', "A little beer, a little beauty,

Representative_Docs:
['@Weaving the Hemp Cloth, Weaving the Hemp Cloth

- Setting up the loom to the sky, catching clouds and humming lullabies  
- The jujube tree drum and the oak siding of the loom house  
- Drum, drum, listen to me, I will open the door for you  
  Do not tie the hemp ropes tightly, please loosen them gently  
- If woven in the day, it’s sunlight hemp cloth; if at night, it’s moonlight hemp cloth  
  Hurry, hurry and weave, the grandmother next door said  
- She came with firewood and asked what the woven cloth was for  
  Our older brother is getting married; I will offer you a green hemp robe  
- What could the man be doing? Weaving and weaving hemp cloth  
  When our lord goes to his bride’s house, we’ll prepare the bridal palanquin  
- Rain, rain, do not come, it will dye the palanquin’s cover  
- The silk skirt will be stained, the satin jeogori will be checked  
- The four legs of the loom are like four brothers  
  The old man playing the drum holds a blue dragon biting a white snake  
- The drum beater’s lamb rattles the thatched cottage all around  
  The lamb that kicks the tangled hemp is twisting the rainbow  
- Like hanging in the sky, three brothers hum lullabies  
  The loom has four legs, like four brothers fixing the heddle  
- The only sons of three generations jump and skip around  
  The three white jade columns ring fully; the one pulling the shuttle  
- As if crossing the Zizi River, hanging by a silver thread from the neck  
  It’s done, it’s done, one bolt of hemp cloth is finished  
- Clack clack, a letter arrived as I was weaving  
  Took it at the front door, opened it at the back door  
  The letter said my mother died  
- Took off my belt, held the letter to my chest, took out the hairpin, stuck it in the ground', 'Setting up the loom in the sky,  
Catching clouds and crying plaintively,  
On the jujube tree drum,  
In the oak bark drum cover,  
Beat the drum, beat the drum, listen to me,  
I will open the door for you.  
Don’t tie the warp tight,  
Please let it flutter loosely.

If woven during the day, it’s sunlight silk,  
If woven at night, it’s moonlight silk.  
Weave quickly, quickly,  
The grandmother from the house behind  
Came with firewood,  
Why does she weave that cloth?  
Our older brother is getting married,  
I will make him a blue hemp garment.  
What’s that man up to?  
Weaving, weaving hemp weaving.

When our elder sister gets married,  
They will make a palanquin robe for her.  
Rain, rain, don’t come,  
The palanquin top will get wet.  
The silk skirt will get stained,  
The satin jacket will get spotted.  

The loom legs are the three brothers,  
These legs here, two legs there,  
The boy beating the drum is like  
A blue dragon holding a white snake,  
The boy striking the drum cover  
Makes the three-room thatched cottage shake.  
The boy twisting the heddle  
Seems to be bending a rainbow,  
Hanging it in the sky,  
The three brothers crying plaintively.  

The loom legs are three brothers,  
The weaving shuttle is their sibling,  
The only son of three generations, feeling restless,  
Makes the white-cotton three-room house ring with sound.  
The boy pulling the thread  
Hangs his neck on a silver cord,  
As if crossing the Yellow River.  

It’s finished, it’s finished,  
One bolt of fabric is finished.  
Snapping and clacking as they weave,  
A letter came, a letter came,  
Received at the front door,  
Opened at the back door,  
The letter says our mother is dead.  
A letter came, a letter came,

Taking off my mourning clothes to hold in my arms,  
Taking out the hairpin to stick into the ground,  
Letting down my hair and tying it roughly,

Striking the ground won’t help.  
After three years of married life,

Always busy with work,  
But now my mother has died,  
My mother has died.  

It’s finished, it’s finished,  
One bolt of fabric is finished.', 'Weave the loom, weave the loom,  
Weave the loom on the jade railing.  
Hey, the weaving maiden sings a love song,  
But in the loom, only worries are woven.  

If woven by day, it is sunlight silk,  
If woven by night, it is moonlight silk.  
Gathering both sunlight silk and moonlight silk,  
Shall I make a shirt for my husband?  

Hey, the weaving maiden sings a love song,  
But in the loom, only worries are woven.  

If an old woman weaves, it is coarse linen,  
If a young woman weaves, it is fine hemp silk.  
Gathering both coarse linen and fine hemp silk,  
Shall I make a shirt for my husband?  

Hey, the weaving maiden sings a love song,  
But in the loom, only worries are woven.']

Representative_Docs:
["The man goes to the beach to the sea  
Puts a shroud on his back  
Wears grave gloves on his hands  
Picks full from the Turkish mantle  
Puts the bigger ones in his mouth  
Throws the smaller ones aside  
They then grow into fish  
Climbed over into big ones  
Multiplied into herring.  
They stood along the sea  
Carried cold from village to village  
Waving in the waves.  
If only, if only, our dear brothers  
If only the sea would give fish  
Deep to catch perch  
Big to shroud over it  
Up, up, oarsmen brothers.  
Up, let's plow the sea  
Deep, let's dig a hole  
Save the edges of the sea  
Cut big nets.  
Then the sea will give fish  
Deep to catch perch  
Big to shroud over it.", 'The life of the sea folk is,
As they, full of tempests.
When their fish is caught,
They bring it into the towns.
When they also go out fishing,
They must endure many storms,
Before the little Pentecost returns.

When they come ashore,
With their small light ships,
They lay the fish on the beach,
Which they then haul into heaps:
This gives the seaman joy,
If the fish still has breath!
But it does not live long.

When the fish is then sold,
They lay it in their bins.
It is brought into the city.
From youth they get used to it,
That they carry this fish:
This is two miles away,
Through dunes and wilderness.

Also, a hundred and fifty pounds,
A strong fisherman can carry:
You can well understand this,
That sweat must pour from him?
When they walk in the city,
They must satisfy their walk:
Many miles around that is.

When they draw fresh fish,
They do this with nets and horses.
The shrimp croaking is among them,
For profit, also high in value:
If no fish is caught,
They lack some money,
Which brings them to catch.

When the sea strikes fiercely,
They cannot catch fish then.
The folk indeed go to their doom,
When they then go their ways,
To catch its fish:
Where the sea is nearly full of it,
In its fury.

They care much for their village,
They would not part from it,
Even if their share could be
In another better time.
When they sail from the coast,
They fish also with pleasure,
Even if they have no rest.

The great sea also sweeps wildly,
As they sail on its waves:
Wild is also the wild beast:
So is the sea folk in their life.
Flocks is their daily work.
When they come out of church,
They mostly drink strong.

Lying is also their nature,
When they deal with your trades.
When they are joyful,
They speak many foolish words.
It seems they are free
From thievery in selling,
Although they overpromise.
Net weaving is the work,
For those who do not want to catch fish.
They also do not play very strongly,
In their reckless ways?
They go out fishing for herring.
They like whale hunting,
No matter how rough the sea may be.

Can a seaman be pious?
Why should it not be possible,
When they sail on the stream,
That they would not fear God?
Fishermen can be pious,
Though there is little appearance of it,
That their mind is pure.

When the storm rages very long,
This gives them bad times:
God the Lord does this lightly,
To lead these people to Him:
If they had understanding of this,
They lightly sailed from the shore,
To the eternal Fatherland.', 'You threw the thousand-fathom fishing line right into the middle of the great Daecheon Sea.  
Quietly, quietly, surely biting, only one bit.

Quietly, quietly, quietly, quietly,  
Pressed down in the winter squash, struggling to wiggle.

Sigh, oh, this is for sure a true bite. I have to bait it again and cast it again.

Quietly, quietly,  
Bite once more for the real catch.

Quietly, quietly, where is the real bite? Bite the hairtail fish (NG).  
(No sound up to here)  

Ah, the hairtail fishing line, right in the middle of the great Daecheon Sea,  
Blowing this sound, blowing that sound, awakening Hanyang from sleep,  
Come to your senses, the hairtail fishing line.  
Gangnam Sea’s hairtail fish,  
This sea, this hairtail,  
Where are you going? Why not bite this fishing line? Where are you going?  
If you clash, you too hold tight, and I hold tight too.  
Where are you going? If there’s a fish with a front tooth missing,

Dive into this fishing line. Where are you going that you don’t come?

I stay up all night watching you.  
Quietly, quietly, if it bites firmly hold and give it a pull.  
Pressed down in the winter squash, struggling to wiggle,  
"Where are you going? Why don’t you bite? Bite firmly."  
Quietly, quietly,  
“Oh my, this bit firmly. You too hold tight, I too hold tight, let’s try once more. Try once more. Oh, this is for sure a true bite. Oh, this will sell well,  
I can buy rice for my family with this, make a living and have a livelihood.  
Ah, again bait it and cast again.”  
Quietly, quietly, when it bites hold tight, you hold tight, I hold tight,  
“Bite firmly. Oh, it bit again. Let’s try again. Oh, this is also a true bite.

The moon rises, the moon rises, in the rivers and lakes room the moon rises.  
Where has Mr. Gangho gone, does he not know the moon has risen?  
He has fallen, fallen into the concubine’s room.

On the way for three or four days, he hurried even before noon.  
A woman who looks like lightning swiftly flew in,  
and bows like a fluttering butterfly.  
If even women’s eyes see this, how sorrowful must it be for a man’s eyes?

Please accept this cup of liquor, our house is hard to visit,  
discard the silver cup and brass cup, accept this cup in a simple cup.

The warp beam of the loom is like a second brother, the weft beam is like a fourth brother,  
the yarn beam is a second brother too, and the eyebrow beam is an old widower.

planned to part at the small festive party, but I couldn’t go because of dancing.

parents like heaven, a wife like an inspector,  
a son with a topknot, and a daughter in the house,

If he, stubborn, lazy or wicked,  
Has committed a bad deed?

“Therefore I sing,  
Therefore I jump,”  
Says little Jet while dancing,  
Who sets her little feet with pleasure.  
Who steadily must stay at school,  
To him, by all appearances,  
Reading and writing  
Will soon be tiresome.

Sometimes banishing worry,  
Makes one cheerful and content.  
A bow too strongly drawn,  
Easily snaps apart.

Blessed are we that learning,  
Free from slavish torment,  
If we work diligently,  
Is replaced by play!

Then one sees us content,  
When recess is over,  
Again happily stepping to school,  
Then the song rings out again joyfully:

“Playing all day  
Would, by all appearances,  
Bore us eventually;  
There must be variety.”  
There went a little man over the bridge,  
With seven cats on his back,  
And each cat had seven kittens:  
Ra, ra, how many legs went over the bridge?  
Two-legs sat on three-legs,  
Then came four-legs and wanted to bite three-legs,  
Then two-legs took three-legs,  
To throw at four-legs with it.  
Whitie, whitie sat on the rack,  
Whitie, whitie broke his neck,  
And there is no carpenter  
Who can fix whitie, whitie.  
There stands a lady in the door,  
With a white kerchief in front,  
The more she stands there,  
The more she fades away.  
A wooden little house,  
A copper little safe,  
An iron turn in the hole:  
Ra, ra, what is that?"]

From early morning until late at night  
We always live in luxury,  
But I never had more pleasure  
Than when I became a Musketeer.  
My first Garrison you want to know,  
That was Breda, that beautiful City,  
Where I had much amusement,  
Especially with the girls of Breda,  
But the joy was almost over,  
Then we had to go march.  
Then you could see the girls crying,  
Because we had to leave,  
For they were heavily burdened,

You will have Soldiers here again,  
To do as you wish,  
Because they carry the same Sabers,  
To stab you once,  
That does not hurt the girls.

Merrily dancing with the Hostesses,  
Both day and night,  
Satisfied with their desire by our strength.

So do not be angry with us.

We are already coming to the Walloon coast,  
Set your youth at ease,  
There life is very affordable,  
With our money, we make pleasure,  
And drink wine and beer.

Play on drums and flute,  
Make such a sweet sound.  
Our Major rides a horse  
And we soldiers all together  
Follow behind.

And gave us so sweet winks,  
Our heart seemed through the love fire,  
Almost about to faint.  
How can life be better,  
Because we have it as we wish,  
Dressed just like a banner Lord,  
And with so many young girls,  
Whom we have for pleasure,  
Because they love Soldiers.  
All with leave, we now step,  
Back again to our beautiful Holland,  
The girls take the prize,  
Those are the ones we will marry,  
Because above all lands fair,  
Holland takes the prize.  
He who sang this little song  
Was a lad from The Hague,  
He liked the girls very much,  
He made this little song,  
Right out of his head and love glow,  
Because he was full of Soldiers' blood.']

['1. The Christmas holidays have come, let us be merry, the Christmas holidays have come, let us be merry! Carolers are walking around, giving honor and praise, whoever gives them a generous carol, they sing nicely.  
2. And when I heard them, I immediately went among them, and when I heard them, I immediately went among them. First, I go to the living room, to get the most, and a few groshes from your pocket into my corner.  
3. I came to you for caroling, give me some cakes, I haven’t eaten any yet this year and almost cry. My dear housewife, come first to the hall and give me some cake before someone sees me.  
4. Someone gives me one cake, someone maybe two, but since yeast is very bad now, they see that it’s before the holidays, they pour water into it, then people sell it off, and suffer losses from it.  
5. But someone bakes a good number of nice cakes, and I, with great anger, ran away from the oven [...] I close this song, bidding you farewell.', "Carol, carol, Stephen,  
what are you carrying in the jug?  
I carry, I carry a carol,  
I slipped on the ice with it,  
dogs gathered around me,  
they ate my carol.  
I am a little caroler,  
I came to you for a treat,  
give me a treat,  
don't laugh at me.  
I'm not driving a cart,  
whatever you give me, I will take.  
If you give me a piece of honey,  
I'll travel even better,  
God will reward you  
in the garden, in the field.", "Christmas Carols. a) About the Birth of Christ. These carols are performed on St. Stephen's Day, i.e., December 26; children go from house to house, singing them at the door, after which the host or hostess gives them small gifts. Their content is either secular or religious. Secular. 1. Carol, carol, Stephen! what are you carrying in the jug? I am carrying, carrying a carol, I slipped on the ice with it, dogs gathered around me, they ate my carol; 1) what sad thing should I do? I must beg for another. Give me a carol, just don't laugh at me! They gave me a carol, yet they laughed at me. 1) gentlemen, give another, this one cover with mud."]

Name: 40_deer_hunting_hunter_little song
Representative_Docs: ['Green little hunter, what is running out of the cabbage? Running, running is a little roe deer, a black-eyed girl, little hunter, shoot her for me!', 'We will go hunting, hunting, my comrade, my, my, my, my comrade: hunting, hunting, through the pine grove, my comrade, my, my, my, my comrade! The hare is running, running, my comrade: let’s release the hounds, so they catch the hare, my comrade! The roe deer is running, running, my comrade: let’s release the hounds, so they catch the doe, my comrade! The deer is running, running, my comrade: let’s release the hounds, so they catch the young buck, my comrade! The maiden is running, running, my comrade: let’s release the hounds, so they catch the maiden, my comrade! We will share, share, my comrade: you get the hare and the doe, I get the young buck and the maiden, my comrade! If you think that’s too little, too little, my comrade: you get all the game and I get the charming girl, my comrade!', 'Waiting. There is nothing better in the world than a green grove: when that beautiful little moon clears up above it! And here I am with my beloved, waiting again for wild game, for wild game, for roe deer, stags, and hares. A hare runs through the valley, a roe deer runs through the grove; the little hare approaches my maiden, he does not know her. "I shot at the hare, only that I missed him: oh, my dear God, how I aimed! Teach me, little hunter, teach me to shoot: I want to gladly reward you for it sometime. I will shoot a roe deer for you, give you a beautiful little kiss; you will be happy about it, we will both have enough." Záb. mysl I, 50, 51.']
